## Lab 1 

Load the dataset "mpg" and work through the exercises below. Note, "mpg" is included in the tidyverse package, so you will need to load the package first.

1. Calculate the **mean**, **range**, **minimum**, and **maximum** of the variable "hwy" across all models. Then, combine these statistics into one vector. (Tip: look up the RDocumentation for the functions `mean`, `range`, `min`, and `max`).

```{r} 

library(tidyverse)
data(mpg)

mean_hwy <- mean(mpg$hwy)
range_hwy <- range(mpg$hwy)
min_hwy <- min(mpg$hwy)
max_hwy <- max(mpg$hwy)
sum_stats <- c(mean_hwy, range_hwy, min_hwy, max_hwy) 
sum_stats
```

2. Since "hwy" is measured in miles per gallon, create a new variable in mpg that expresses "hwy" in litres per 100 km. 

```{r} 

temp <- 235.215 / mpg$hwy
mpg$hwy_Lp100km_1 <- temp

# Or, in one step
mpg$hwy_Lp100km_2 <- 235.215 / mpg$hwy

unique(mpg$hwy_Lp100km_1 == mpg$hwy_Lp100km_2) # sanity check
```

3. Identify the models of cars that are most fuel-efficient. Which classes of cars are least fuel-efficient? 

```{r} 

mpg$model[mpg$hwy == max(mpg$hwy)]

mpg$class[mpg$hwy_Lp100km_1 == max(mpg$hwy_Lp100km_1)]

unique(mpg$class[mpg$hwy_Lp100km_1 == max(mpg$hwy_Lp100km_1)]) # using unique function to remove duplicates
```

4. Compute the quantiles of "hwy". Can you also calculate the tertiles instead? (Tip: look up for the RDocumentation for the function `quantile`).

```{r}

quantile(mpg$hwy)

quantile(mpg$hwy, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.333)) 
quantile(mpg$hwy, c(0, 0.333, 0.666, 1)) # you can achieve the same using this
```

5. Now, based on the tertiles you calculated, assign "least efficient", "medium", and "most efficient" labels to all models. Try using both base R indexing and the function `ifelse`.

```{r}

tertile <- quantile(mpg$hwy, c(0, 0.333, 0.666, 1))

mpg$efficient_class_1 <- NA # optional, this eliminates the warning message of "Unknown or uninitialised column"
mpg$efficient_class_1[mpg$hwy < tertile[2]] <- "least efficient"
mpg$efficient_class_1[mpg$hwy >= tertile[2] & mpg$hwy < tertile[3]] <- "medium"
mpg$efficient_class_1[mpg$hwy >= tertile[3]] <- "most efficient"

# OR
mpg$efficient_class_2 <- NA # given how ifelse functions are specified below, this step becomes necessary
mpg$efficient_class_2 <- ifelse(mpg$hwy < tertile[2], "least efficient", mpg$efficient_class_2)
mpg$efficient_class_2 <- ifelse(mpg$hwy >= tertile[2] & mpg$hwy < tertile[3], "medium", mpg$efficient_class_2)
mpg$efficient_class_2 <- ifelse(mpg$hwy >= tertile[3], "most efficient", mpg$efficient_class_2)

unique(mpg$efficient_class_1 == mpg$efficient_class_2) # sanity check
```

Continue from the farm business dataset "farm" used in Lab 2, work through the exercises below.

  1. Create a new variable called **size3** that meets the following criteria: 
  
      i) size3 = “small” if size <= 200
    
      ii) size3 = “medium” if 200 < size <= 600
    
      iii) size3 = “big” if size > 600
    
      Finally, convert size3 to a factor variable that is ordinal from "small" to "big".  
  
```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false

name <- c("Henry", "Larry", "Alex", "Gaby", "Amy", "Ruby")
sex <- c("male", "male", "male", "female", "female", "female")
age <- c(43, 60, 25, 50, 28, 58) 
type <- c("crop", "livestock", "urban", "dairy", "crop", "livestock") 
size <- c(550, 800, 10, 600, 1000, 700) 
return <- c(40, 90, 50, 90, 90, 95)

farm <- data.frame(name, age, sex, type, size, return)
 
farm <- farm %>% mutate(size3 = ifelse(size <= 200, "small", NA)) %>%
                 mutate(size3 = ifelse(size > 200 & size <= 600, "medium", size3)) %>%
                 mutate(size3 = ifelse(size > 600, "big", size3)) %>%
                 mutate(size3 = factor(size3, levels = c("small", "medium", "big")))

farm
farm$size3  

```
 
  2. Generate the following summary statistics, for each type of the farms:
  
      i) the sum of all returns, called **tot.return**
    
      ii) the average returns, called **avg.return**
    
      Finally, rearrange the data based on the value of avg.return, in the descending order.
  
```{r}
#| warning: false
#| message: false

farm.sum <- farm %>% group_by(type) %>%
                     summarize(tot.return = sum(return), 
                               avg.return = mean(return))
```


## Lab 3 

Continue from your multiple linear regression "mod2":

1. Calculate the R-squared using $y_i$ and $\hat{y}_i$, that is
  $$
  R^2 = corr(y_i, \hat{y}_i)^2
  $$
  (tip: you can retrieve the fitted values $\hat{y}_i$ via `mod2$fitted.values`.)
  
```{r}

wage <- read.csv(file = "D:/Dropbox/Teaching/AREC513/Fall2025/materials/data/ch2_data_csv/wages1.csv") 
mod2 <- lm(wage ~ male + school + exper, data = wage)
sum_mod2 <- summary(mod2)

y     <- wage$wage
yhat  <- mod2$fitted.values
R2_via_corr <- cor(y, yhat)^2
R2_via_corr

```

2. Construct the confidence interval for $\hat{\beta}_{male}$, with the significance level of 10%.

```{r}

ci_male_90 <- confint(mod2, parm = "male", level = 0.90)
ci_male_90

```

{{< pagebreak >}}

3. Test $H_0:\beta_{exper} = 0.15$,  with the significance level of 10%. 

```{r}

beta_exper <- sum_mod2$coefficients["exper","Estimate"]
se_exper   <- sum_mod2$coefficients["exper","Std. Error"]
df         <- mod2$df.residual
t_stat     <- (beta_exper - 0.15) / se_exper

t_crit <-  qt(1 - 0.10 / 2, df)
t_stat >= t_crit   # gives False, hence do not reject H0

```

4. Test $H_0:\beta_{school} + \beta_{exper} = 0.75$,  with the significance level of 1%.

```{r}
#| message: false

library(car)
linearHypothesis(mod2, c("school + exper = 0.75"))   # do not reject H0, given the F stats or p-value

```

5. Predict the wage per hour for a male worker with 18 years of schooling and 0 years of experience.

```{r} 

pred_data <- data.frame(male = 1, school = 18, exper = 0)

predict(mod2, newdata = pred_data)

```

2. Why does the Sargan Test report NA values for object "diag_iv"?

```
Because Sargan Test is for the over-identified case, where the number of IVs is larger than the number of endogeneous variables.
```

## Lab 5

Use the following dataset on 10 farmers that:

- a potential profit $profit^1$ is realized if the new technology is adopted, otherwise $profit^0$

- the counterfactual is observable

Answer Question 1 and 2.

```{r}
farmer_id <- 1 : 10
profit_state1 <- c(120, 90, 90, 150, 80, 160, 60, 95, 100, 75)    # adoption of the technology
profit_state0 <- c(100, 95, 85, 110, 90, 100, 70, 90, 80, 100)    # no adoption
```
 
1. Suppose the farmers will only adopt the technology if it is profitable, generate the dummy variable "d_adopt".

```{r}
df_farm <- data.frame(farmer_id, profit_state1, profit_state0)
df_farm <- df_farm %>% mutate(d_adopt = ifelse(profit_state1 > profit_state0, 1, 0)) 
```

2. Calculate $ATE$, $ATT$, $ATU$, and show that $ATE$ is the weighted average of the other two terms.

```{r} 
ATE <- mean(df_farm$profit_state1) - mean(df_farm$profit_state0)

treated_farm <- df_farm %>% filter(d_adopt == 1)  
ATT <- mean(treated_farm$profit_state1) - mean(treated_farm$profit_state0)

untreated_farm <- df_farm %>% filter(d_adopt == 0)  
ATU <- mean(untreated_farm$profit_state1) - mean(untreated_farm$profit_state0)

c(ATE = ATE, ATT = ATT, ATU = ATU)
```

Now, imagine a more realistic situation where the counterfactual is not observable, and only the realized profits and whether the farms adopted the technology can be observed. 

Create this new data frame and answer Question 3 through 5.

3. Calculate the $ODM$ and verify that the regression results correspond to it.

```{r}
ODM <- mean(df_farm$profit_state1[df_farm$d_adopt == 1]) - mean(df_farm$profit_state0[df_farm$d_adopt == 0])
ODM

df_farm <- df_farm %>% mutate(profit_obs = ifelse(d_adopt == 1, profit_state1, profit_state0))

reg_farm <- lm(profit_obs ~ d_adopt, data = df_farm)
summary(reg_farm) 
```

4. Calculate the selection bias and the heterogeneous treatment effects bias.

```{r}

treated_state0_profit   <- mean(treated_farm$profit_state0)
untreated_state0_profit <- mean(untreated_farm$profit_state0) 

selection_bias <- treated_state0_profit - untreated_state0_profit
selection_bias

# ATT + selection_bias == ODM => TRUE
```

5. Simulate a sample of 10,000 observations by repeatedly using the same 10 observations on the farmers, with only 6 out of 10 farmers adopt the technology randomly each time. Show that when estimating a regression, the coefficient of "d_adopt" approaches the true ATE.

```{r}
set.seed(1)

df_base <- function() {
  data.frame(profit_state1, profit_state0) %>% 
    mutate(
      d_adopt = ifelse(row_number() %in% sample(10, 6), 1, 0),
      profit_obs = ifelse(d_adopt == 1, profit_state1, profit_state0)
```

## Lab 6

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| echo: false

options(scipen = 9999) # turn off scientific notation

library(dplyr)  

# package for RDD
library(ggplot2)
library(rdrobust)
library(rddensity)

# package for DiD and event study
library(fixest)

## preparation

set.seed(100) 

### RDD

df_rdd <- data.frame(score = rnorm(1000, 100, 50)) %>% mutate(score = ifelse(score < 0, 0, score)) %>%
  filter(score <= 240)

u <- rnorm(nrow(df_rdd), 0, 1000) # noise
 
df_rdd <- df_rdd %>% 
  mutate(
    D  = ifelse(score > 120, 1, 0), # policy cutoff at score = 120
    score2 = score * score,
    earn0 = 10000 + 0 * D - 100 * score + score2 + u,
      
    score_center = score - 120,
    score_center2 = score_center * score_center
  )

df_rdd <- df_rdd %>% 
  mutate(
    earn1 = earn0 + 5000,
    earn_ob = ifelse(D == 1, earn1, earn0),
    score_center3 = score_center * score_center * score_center
  )

### DiD

years <- 2000:2020
provinces <- c("A", "B")

df_did <- expand.grid(year = years, province = provinces)

df_did <- df_did %>%
  mutate(
    unemp_base = ifelse(province == "A", 13, 10),
    trend = -0.1 * (year - 2000),
    unemp_0 = unemp_base + trend + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.05),
    
    jt_effect = ifelse(province == "A" & year >= 2010, -2, 0),
    unemp_ob = unemp_0 + jt_effect
  )

df_did <- df_did %>% mutate(
  post = ifelse(year >= 2010, 1, 0),
  treat = ifelse(province == "A", 1, 0),
  post_treat = post * treat
)
did_simple <- lm(unemp_ob ~ treat + post + post_treat, data = df_did)

cities <- c("a", "b", "c", "d")

df_did2 <- expand.grid(year = years, city = cities)

df_did2 <- df_did2 %>%
  mutate(
    unemp_base = case_when(city == "a" ~ 13, city == "b" ~ 11, city == "c" ~ 10, city == "d" ~ 7),
    trend = -0.1 * (year - 2000),
    unemp_0 = unemp_base + trend + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.05),
    province = ifelse(city == "a" | city == "b", "A", "B"),
    
    jt_effect = ifelse(province == "A" & year >= 2010, -2, 0),
    unemp_ob = unemp_0 + jt_effect
  )
```

## Matching and Subclassification

Suppose the rating of "performance" (High/Medium/Low) is derived from a comprehensive index ranging between 0 and 100, explain in reality (having no prior knowledge on the data generation process) why we may have the "Curse of Dimensionality" problem. 

When performance is measured on a 0–100 continuous scale, exact matching becomes nearly impossible. If we discretize the variable into small bins (e.g., width of 5 or 10), some bins may contain no observations or only controls or only treated units. The problem would become worse once additional covariates are included.
 
## Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD)

1. Use the linear regression as the example to explain why we need to center $Score_i$ first to identify $\delta$ as the treatment effect. 

Recall that, the linear regression estimates
$$
Earn_i = \alpha + \delta D_i + \beta_{1} \tilde{Score_i} + \gamma_{1}(D_i * \tilde{Score_i}) + \epsilon_i, \text{where } \tilde{Score_i} = Score_i - 120
$$

At cutoff, the centered $Score_i$ equals 0,

- At the left limit (untreated):
$$
\lim_{\tilde{Score_i} \rightarrow 0}E[Earn_i^0|\tilde{Score_i}=0] = \alpha
$$

- At the right limit (treated):
$$
\lim_{\tilde{Score_i} \leftarrow 0}E[Earn_i^1 | \tilde{Score_i} = 0] = \alpha + \delta
$$

Hence, it makes $\delta$, the coefficient of $D_i$, capturing the treatment effect, as
$$
\delta = E[Earn_i^1 - Earn_i^0 | \tilde{Score_i}=0] 
$$

2. Estimate a similar polynomial regression but include the term with order 3?

```{r}
rdd_poly3 <- lm(earn_ob ~ D + 
                  score_center  + D:score_center  + 
                  score_center2 + D:score_center2 + 
                  score_center3 + D:score_center3,
                data = df_rdd)
summary(rdd_poly3)

```

3. To show robustness, perform multiple placebo tests at other alternative cutoffs.

```{r}
rdr_1 <- rdrobust(y = df_rdd$earn_ob, x = df_rdd$score, c = 90) 
rdr_2 <- rdrobust(y = df_rdd$earn_ob, x = df_rdd$score, c = 150)

coef <- c(cutoff_90  = rdr_1$coef[1], cutoff_150 = rdr_2$coef[1])
p_value <- c(cutoff_90  = rdr_1$pv[1], cutoff_150 = rdr_2$pv[1])

data.frame(coef = coef, p_value = p_value)
```
 
## Difference-in-Differences (DiD)

1. Use the results of the DiD regression ("did_simple"), calculate the average pre-treatment and post-treatment unemployment for province A and province B.

Recall the estimated regression,
$$
\text{unemp}_{it} = \alpha + \beta\text{Treat}_i+\gamma\text{Post}_t + \delta\bigg( \text{Post}_t \times \text{Treat}_i \bigg) + \epsilon_{it}
$$

- For province B ($\text{Treat}_i = 0$) and pre-treatment ($\text{Post}_t = 0$):
$\text{unemp}_{B,pre} = \alpha$

- For province B ($\text{Treat}_i = 0$) and post-treatment ($\text{Post}_t = 1$):
$\text{unemp}_{B,post} = \alpha + \gamma$

- For province A ($\text{Treat}_i = 1$) and pre-treatment ($\text{Post}_t = 0$):
$\text{unemp}_{A,pre} = \alpha + \beta$

- For province A ($\text{Treat}_i = 1$) and post-treatment ($\text{Post}_t = 1$):
$\text{unemp}_{A,post} = \alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta$

```{r}
alpha <- did_simple$coefficients["(Intercept)"]
beta  <- did_simple$coefficients["treat"]
gamma <- did_simple$coefficients["post"]
delta <- did_simple$coefficients["post_treat"]

B_pre  <- alpha
B_post <- alpha + gamma
A_pre  <- alpha + beta
A_post <- alpha + beta + gamma + delta

c(B_pre = unname(B_pre), B_post = unname(B_post), A_pre = unname(A_pre), A_post = unname(A_post))
```

4. In the visualization for results of the event study ("event_study"), is the parallel trends assumption satisfied?
 
Yes. given that the pre-treatment coefficients are around zero and statistically insignificant, the pattern supports the validity of the parallel trends assumption.
